pages.name: Powers of ten
pages.text: This is the [[power ruler]]. Its big marks on top are 1, 10, 100 and 1000, each ten times the one before, at equal spaces, with their powers of 10 underneath. One space right multiplies the number by 10 and adds 1 to the power. So `10³ = 1000`, and asked the other way round, the power 10 needs to make 1000 is 3. That power is the [[logarithm]], `log₁₀ 1000 = 3`, the 3 in kilo's 10³. Drag the pointer.

pages.name: Which log?
pages.task: `10⁴ = 10 000`. Which says the same thing as a logarithm?
pages.why: A logarithm is the power the base needs to make the number. The base is 10, the number 10 000 and the power 4, so `log₁₀ 10 000 = 4`. The number goes inside the log, and the power comes out.

pages.name: Between the marks
pages.text: Between the marks the same rule holds. Half a space multiplies by `√10 ≈ 3.162`, the number that times itself makes 10, so 316 sits half way from 100 to 1000, at 2.5. Equal lengths multiply by equal factors, so the numbers bunch up towards the right of each space. The magnified space shows 2, 3 and 5 at 0.301, 0.477 and 0.699: `3 × 3 = 9` is just under 10, so 3 sits just under half way. The pointer stops at 45, at 1.653.

pages.name: Where 5 sits
pages.task: On the ruler of 10s, where does 5 sit between 1 and 10? Give its power.
pages.why: Equal lengths multiply by equal factors, so half way is only `√10 ≈ 3.162` and 5 sits further on. Ten 2s multiplied make 1024, just over 10³, so one × 2 step is about 0.3 of a space, and 2 sits at 0.301. 5 is 10 ÷ 2, one × 2 step back from 10, so it sits at `1 − 0.301 = 0.699`. Check by turning it round: `10^0.699 ≈ 5`.

pages.name: The ruler of 2s
pages.text: Any positive base other than 1 makes its own ruler. On the ruler of 2s each space multiplies by 2, so 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 sit at 0 to 5: `log₂ 8 = 3` and `log₂ 32 = 5`. A log is a length along the ruler, and a number like any other, so two of them simply add: `log₂ 8 + log₂ 8 = 3 + 3 = 6`. Flip the switch to compare rulers.

pages.name: A log is a number
pages.task: Say x = 2. Is `log₂ x + log₂ x + log₂ x` the same as `x + x + x`?
pages.why: A log is a length along the ruler, and a number like any other. `log₂ 2 = 1`, so three of them make `1 + 1 + 1 = 3`, while `2 + 2 + 2 = 6`. The log cannot be dropped as if it were not there.

pages.name: The ruler of e
pages.text: The number e, about 2.71828, makes a ruler too. Each space multiplies by e, so its marks are 1, 2.718, 7.389 and 20.09. Its log is the [[natural logarithm]], written ln, so `ln 7.389 ≈ 2`. On a calculator, and in this course, the log key means base 10 and the ln key base e. Any other base is written, as in log₂ 8. Flip the switch: the same power sits under a different number on each ruler.

pages.name: Natural log of 10
pages.task: On the ruler of e, 10 sits between 7.389 and 20.09. What is ln 10?
pages.why: ln 10 asks what power of e makes 10. 10 is between `e² ≈ 7.389` and `e³ ≈ 20.09`, so the answer is between 2 and 3, and the ln key gives 2.303. On the ruler of 10s, 10 sits at 1. ln and log give different answers for every number except 1, which sits at power 0 on every ruler, because any base to the power 0 is 1, as in Powers and roots.

pages.name: Left of 1
pages.text: Go left of 1 and the powers go negative. 0.1 is 10⁻¹, one over 10, so `log 0.1 = −1`, and 0.01 sits at −2 and 0.001 at −3. Each space left divides by 10 again, so the numbers shrink towards 0 but never reach it, because a positive base to any power is positive. So 0 and the negative numbers have no mark, and no logarithm among ordinary numbers.

pages.name: A negative number
pages.why: A logarithm asks what power of 10 makes the number. Going left, the numbers shrink towards 0 but never reach it: every power of 10 is positive. So no power of 10 makes −100, and a calculator gives an error. A small positive number does have a log: `log 0.01 = −2`.

pages.name: The fold
pages.text: Asking the question the other way round swaps the input and the output. The graph of `y = eˣ` passes through `(0, 1)`, `(1, 2.718)` and `(2, 7.389)`. Fold it over the dashed line `y = x` and each point swaps its two numbers, so `(1, 2.718)` lands on `(2.718, 1)`. The folded curve is `y = ln x`, just as you undid machines in Functions and their graphs. So ln undoes eˣ: `ln(e²) = 2`.

pages.task: `y = eˣ` passes through `(2, 7.389)`. Which point does the fold over `y = x` put on `y = ln x`?
pages.why: The fold swaps the two numbers of every point, so `(2, 7.389)` lands on `(7.389, 2)`. It says `ln 7.389 ≈ 2`: the power e needs to make 7.389 is 2, since `e² ≈ 7.389`.
